data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more likely true, but as a methodological rule to maximize the 'degree of corroboration' which serves as a report of past performance without predicting future success; however, accepting this defense costs the scientist any rational assurance that acting on the preferred theory will yield successful practical outcomes, reducing scientific action to a non-rational 'leap' or pragmatic bet that implicitly relies on the very uniformity of nature Popper explicitly rejected.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration is strictly a report of the past, it cannot logically guide future action without assuming the future resembles the past (induction).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper advocates choosing the better-corroborated theory for action, he is implicitly assigning it higher subjective probability despite his explicit denial.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice is merely a 'bet,' then Popper's philosophy offers no rational advantage over irrationalism or conventionalism regarding practical application.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Distinction between logical probability (induction) and methodological preference (corroboration report), coupled with the admission that practical action requires an extra-logical decision.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
